question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word ‘fertile’ in the given sentence.
The teacher asked, “Wheat is grown in which kind of land – rich, wet, barren and fecund?”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Barren.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Fertile" means land or soil that is rich and able to produce good crops or vegetation. Its antonym is "Barren", which means land that is not fertile enough to support the growth of plants or crops. (बंजर)
◦ Example: Farmers avoided settling near the barren land because nothing would grow there.

• In the given sentence, the teacher lists four kinds of land — rich, wet, barren and fecund — and asks which kind wheat grows in; the antonym relationship is between "fertile" (in the question stem) and one of the listed words, i.e. "barren".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Fecund" is incorrect because fecund is a synonym of fertile, meaning capable of producing abundant vegetation or offspring. (उपजाऊ)

• Option 2: "Rich" is incorrect because rich land, like fertile land, is productive and full of nutrients — it is a synonym, not an antonym, of fertile.

• Option 4: "Wet" is incorrect because wetness of soil is unrelated to fertility; wet land is not necessarily infertile, so it cannot serve as the antonym of fertile.

NOTE

• Other common synonyms of fertile: fecund, fruitful, productive, prolific.

• Other common antonyms of fertile: barren, sterile, arid, unproductive.

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
The manager explained the latest assignment to Lana.
option_1: The latest assignment was explained to Lana by the manager.
option_2: The latest assignment had explained to Lana by the manager.
option_3: The latest assignment had been explained to Lana by the manager.
option_4: The latest assignment had been explain to Lana by the manager.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The latest assignment was explained to Lana by the manager.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The manager explained the latest assignment to Lana" is in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the latest assignment" becomes the subject; being singular, the auxiliary used is "was"; the verb "explained" becomes the past participle "explained" (V3); and "the manager" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The latest assignment was explained to Lana by the manager.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "had explained" is an active-voice Past Perfect form, not a valid passive structure; the passive requires a form of "be" plus the past participle.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "had been explained" is the passive of the Past Perfect Tense, which is not the tense of the given active sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because the verb form "explain" should be the past participle "explained"; "had been explain" is grammatically wrong.

NOTE

• Always identify the tense of the active sentence first, since the passive auxiliary and participle form depend entirely on it.

• Common confusion: students often mix Past Perfect ("had been + V3") with Simple Past ("was/were + V3") passives — check the time clues in the active sentence carefully.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Transient
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Temporary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Transient" means lasting only for a short time; not permanent. Its synonym is "Temporary", which also means existing or continuing for a limited time. (अस्थायी/क्षणिक)
◦ Example: The pain from the injection was transient and disappeared within minutes.

• Both words describe something that does not last, as opposed to something permanent or enduring.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Transform" (रूपांतरित करना): means to change completely in form or appearance; it is unrelated in meaning to "transient".

• Option 3: "Transmit" (प्रसारित करना): means to send or pass something (such as a signal, disease, or information) from one place/person to another.

• Option 4: "Trap" (जाल): means a device or trick used to catch someone/something, or a difficult situation one cannot escape; it has no connection with "temporary".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of transient: fleeting, momentary, short-lived, ephemeral, passing.

• Antonym of transient: permanent, enduring, everlasting.

question:
Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.
She asked me why I had been smoking that day.
option_1: She said to me, “Why were you smoking today?”
option_2: She said to me, “Why are you smoking today?”
option_3: She said to me, “Why you smoke today?”
option_4: She says to me, “Why were you smoking this day?”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. She said to me, "Why were you smoking today?"

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given indirect sentence uses the reporting verb "asked" (past tense) and the reported verb "had been smoking", which is the Past Perfect Continuous tense.

• Rule — converting Indirect to Direct speech:
◦ When the reporting verb is in the past tense, the tense of the reported speech in indirect form is one step behind the original direct-speech tense (this is called backshifting); to recover the direct form, the tense must be shifted forward by one step.
◦ Past Perfect Continuous (indirect) → Past Continuous (direct): "had been smoking" → "were smoking".
◦ Pronoun "me" (indirect, referring to the listener) → "you" (direct, since the speaker addresses the listener directly).
◦ Time expression "that day" (indirect) → "today" (direct), since indirect speech shifts "today" to "that day" when reported later.
◦ Since it is a Wh-question, the reporting verb becomes "said to" and the question mark and question-word order are restored inside quotation marks.

• Applying the rule: "She asked me why I had been smoking that day" → She said to me, "Why were you smoking today?"

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "are you smoking" (Present Continuous) does not correctly reverse the backshift from "had been smoking" (Past Perfect Continuous); the correct direct tense is Past Continuous, not Present Continuous.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "you smoke" loses the continuous aspect entirely and also fails to form a grammatically correct question (missing auxiliary "did/were").

• Option 4 is incorrect because the reporting verb "says" (present tense) is wrong — the original reporting verb "asked" is in the past tense, so the direct form must also use a past reporting verb ("said"); also "this day" is not the correct reverse of "that day".

NOTE

• Common tense backshift pairs (Indirect → Direct): Present Continuous → Past Continuous, Present Perfect → Past Perfect, Simple Past → Past Perfect, Past Continuous → Past Perfect Continuous.

• Common word changes: today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, yesterday→the day before, now→then, here→there, this→that.

question:
Choose the option that can substitute the underlined segment correctly and complete the meaning of the sentence.

Navika is a superb and impressive child in her class.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Brilliant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Brilliant" means exceptionally clever, talented, or outstanding; strikingly impressive. (शानदार/प्रतिभाशाली) It captures both ideas expressed by "superb" (excellent) and "impressive" (remarkable) together, and fits naturally when describing a talented child.
◦ Example: Navika is a brilliant child in her class — she tops every test with ease.

• The underlined segment "superb and impressive" describes Navika's outstanding quality as a student; the single word substitute must convey this combined sense of excellence and being remarkable, which "Brilliant" does most naturally in the context of a person (especially a child/student).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Splendid" (शानदार): means magnificent or very impressive, but it is normally used for things, occasions, or achievements (a splendid view, a splendid performance) rather than to describe a person's inherent quality/character as a student.

• Option 3: "Dazzling" (चकाचौंध करने वाला): means impressively brilliant in a showy, eye-catching way (dazzling lights, a dazzling smile); it suits visual brilliance more than a child's all-round excellence.

• Option 4: "Vivid" (स्पष्ट/जीवंत): means producing powerful, clear images in the mind, or intensely bright in colour; it is used for descriptions, memories, or colours, not for describing a superb and impressive child.

NOTE

• In such "substitute the underlined segment" questions, always check which single word fits BOTH the meaning of the phrase AND the grammatical/contextual slot (here, an adjective describing a person).

• Similar words describing outstanding ability: exceptional, remarkable, outstanding, gifted, prodigious.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.

Casual
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Formal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Casual" means relaxed, informal, or done without much thought or formality. Its antonym is "Formal", which means following established rules, conventions, or etiquette; official and proper. (औपचारिक)
◦ Example: He wore a formal suit to the interview instead of his usual casual clothes.

• Casual and formal represent opposite ends of behaviour, dress, and manner — one relaxed and unofficial, the other structured and official.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Spiritual" (आध्यात्मिक): relates to the human spirit or religion, not to formality; it has no direct opposite relationship with "casual".

• Option 2: "Personal" (व्यक्तिगत): means relating to a particular individual/private matters; it is unrelated to the formal-casual spectrum.

• Option 4: "Traditional" (पारंपरिक): means following long-established customs; while a formal event can also be traditional, "traditional" itself is not the direct antonym of "casual" — "formal" is the precise opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of casual: informal, relaxed, easy-going, offhand.

• Other antonyms of casual: formal, official, ceremonious, proper.

question:
Select the appropriate option to replace the underlined word with the adverb of time.

I went to Paris regularly.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. yesterday.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An adverb of time tells us WHEN an action happens (e.g. today, yesterday, now, soon, later), as distinct from an adverb of frequency, which tells us HOW OFTEN an action happens.

• The underlined word "regularly" is an adverb of frequency, and the question specifically asks for it to be replaced by an adverb of TIME. Among the options, only "yesterday" answers the question "when?", making it the correct adverb of time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Twice" is an adverb of frequency (tells how many times), not an adverb of time.

• Option 2: "Often" is also an adverb of frequency, describing how regularly something happens, not when it happens.

• Option 4: "Happily" is an adverb of manner, describing how an action is performed, unrelated to time or frequency.

NOTE

• Adverbs of time: today, yesterday, tomorrow, now, then, soon, later, already, recently.

• Adverbs of frequency: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never, twice, regularly.

• Adverbs of manner: happily, slowly, carefully, quickly, well.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.

Conceit
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Modesty.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Conceit" means excessive pride in oneself or one's abilities and achievements; vanity. Its antonym is "Modesty", which means a humble or moderate estimation of one's own abilities; not boastful. (विनम्रता)
◦ Example: Despite winning the award, she accepted it with modesty rather than conceit.

• Conceit reflects an inflated sense of self-importance, while modesty reflects humility — the two are direct opposites.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Concealment" (छिपाव): means the act of hiding something; it relates to secrecy, not to pride or humility.

• Option 2: "Reveal" (उजागर करना): means to make something known or visible; it is a verb about disclosure, unrelated to conceit.

• Option 4: "Hidden" (छिपा हुआ): means kept out of sight, again related to concealment rather than to the vanity/humility spectrum of "conceit".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of conceit: vanity, arrogance, pride, self-importance, egotism.

• Other antonyms of conceit: humility, modesty, meekness.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

Feeling or showing extreme tiredness
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Weary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Weary" means feeling or showing extreme tiredness, especially as a result of excessive exertion. (थका हुआ/क्लांत)
◦ Example: After the long trek up the mountain, the climbers were completely weary.

• This is a standard one-word substitution question; the phrase "feeling or showing extreme tiredness" is the dictionary definition of "weary".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Vitalised" (सजीव बनाया गया): means given energy or life; it is the opposite sense — full of energy, not tired.

• Option 2: "Nervous" (घबराया हुआ): means feeling anxious or worried, which is a different emotional state from tiredness.

• Option 4: "Drowsy" (नींद से भरा): means feeling sleepy and lacking alertness; it is close in meaning but specifically denotes sleepiness rather than general extreme tiredness/exhaustion, so it is a weaker fit than "weary".

NOTE

• Other useful one-word substitutes for tiredness-related states: Fatigued (extremely tired), Exhausted (drained of energy completely), Lethargic (sluggish, lacking energy).

• Related one-word substitution practice: "One who works for the love of it, not for money" = Amateur; "A person who has no money" = Pauper.

question:
The question below consists of a set of labeled sentences. Out of the four options given, select the most logical order of the sentences to form a coherent paragraph.
P. We are naturally social creatures.
Q. A bit of solitude—as everyone from Thoreau to Proust have written about—is one of our most powerful tools for disconnecting and recharging.
R. This does not mean you need to lock yourself away in a room at the end of the day.
S. However, all that time with people takes its toll.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. PSQR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence P introduces the general idea: "We are naturally social creatures" — this is the natural opening/topic sentence.

• Sentence S follows P logically using the connector "However", which contrasts with being social: "However, all that time with people takes its toll."

• Sentence Q follows S by introducing the solution to the "toll" mentioned in S: "A bit of solitude...is one of our most powerful tools for disconnecting and recharging."

• Sentence R concludes by clarifying/qualifying the idea of "solitude" introduced in Q: "This does not mean you need to lock yourself away in a room..."

• Applying the rule: the paragraph must move from the general statement (P), to the contrasting problem (S), to the proposed solution (Q), to the clarification of that solution (R) — giving the order P–S–Q–R.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (PQRS) is incorrect because Q (about solitude) cannot directly follow P without S first establishing why solitude is needed (the "toll" of socialising).

• Option 2 (QSRP) is incorrect because it starts with Q (solitude as a tool), before the reader knows why solitude is even necessary — the topic sentence P must come first.

• Option 3 (SPQR) is incorrect because S begins with "However", a contrast word, which cannot logically open the paragraph without a preceding statement (P) for it to contrast with.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always locate the sentence that introduces the topic in general terms (often without pronouns or linking words) — that is usually the opening sentence.

• Words like "however", "this", "this does not mean" are strong clues that a sentence must follow, not lead, the paragraph.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Michael Holding, who
P. 20 years, has finally drawn curtains on
Q. commentary panel for more than
R. was a member of the Sky Sports
S. his stint behind the microphone
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. RQPS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed opening "Michael Holding, who" must be followed by a relative clause describing him, which begins with R: "was a member of the Sky Sports".

• R is naturally followed by Q: "commentary panel for more than", completing the phrase "was a member of the Sky Sports commentary panel for more than".

• Q is followed by P: "20 years, has finally drawn curtains on", giving the duration and the main verb phrase "has finally drawn curtains on".

• Finally, S: "his stint behind the microphone" completes the sentence as the object of "drawn curtains on".

• Applying the rule, the complete sentence reads: "Michael Holding, who was a member of the Sky Sports commentary panel for more than 20 years, has finally drawn curtains on his stint behind the microphone." — giving the order R–Q–P–S.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (QPRS) is incorrect because it places "commentary panel for more than" immediately after "who", which is grammatically incomplete and meaningless without R first.

• Option 3 (SPQR) is incorrect because it starts the relative clause with S ("his stint behind the microphone"), which makes no sense directly after "who".

• Option 4 (PSQR) is incorrect because it starts with P ("20 years, has finally drawn curtains on"), which cannot logically follow "who" without first stating what Michael Holding was (R).

NOTE

• In sentence-rearrangement questions, always find the segment that can grammatically and logically follow the fixed opening/subject first — this quickly eliminates two of the four options.

• The idiom "draw curtains on (something)" means to bring something to an end.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Robin rolled the marble through a small plastic pipe.
option_1: The marble was rolled by Robin in a small plastic pipe.
option_2: A small plastic pipe was rolled through a marble by Robin.
option_3: The marble was rolled through a small plastic pipe by Robin.
option_4: The marble through a small plastic pipe was rolled by Robin.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The marble was rolled through a small plastic pipe by Robin.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Robin rolled the marble through a small plastic pipe" is in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object (+ other elements)
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + (other elements, unchanged in position/order) + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the marble" becomes the subject; being singular, the auxiliary is "was"; the verb "rolled" becomes the past participle "rolled" (V3); the adverbial phrase "through a small plastic pipe" stays attached to the verb in its original position; and "Robin" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The marble was rolled through a small plastic pipe by Robin.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it wrongly places "by Robin" before "in a small plastic pipe" and changes the preposition from "through" to "in", distorting the original meaning.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it swaps the subject and object entirely — making "a small plastic pipe" the subject, which reverses the intended meaning (it was the marble that was rolled, not the pipe).

• Option 4 is incorrect because it awkwardly places the adverbial phrase "through a small plastic pipe" between the subject and the verb, producing an unnatural and non-standard passive construction.

NOTE

• When converting sentences with a prepositional phrase (like "through a pipe", "in a room"), keep that phrase attached to the verb in its original position in the passive sentence — do not let it interrupt the subject-verb-agent structure.

• Only the direct object of a transitive verb becomes the subject in the passive voice; adverbial phrases of place/manner do not become the subject.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.
Bag and baggage
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. With all of one's possessions.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Bag and baggage" means with all of one's belongings/possessions; completely, entirely, leaving nothing behind. (अपना सारा सामान लेकर/पूरी तरह से)
◦ Example: The tenant was asked to vacate the house bag and baggage by the end of the month.

• The phrase originally referred to a soldier's/traveller's full kit and belongings, and today it is used to mean taking absolutely everything one owns when leaving a place.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "With burden" (बोझ के साथ): is a literal, unrelated meaning; the idiom is not about carrying a burden but about carrying all one's possessions.

• Option 2: "Without any aim" (बिना किसी लक्ष्य के): describes aimlessness, which has no connection to the idiom "bag and baggage".

• Option 3: "Without happiness" (खुशी के बिना): describes an emotional state unrelated to the idiom's actual meaning of taking all one's belongings.

NOTE

• Other common SSC idioms with "bag": "In the bag" (certain to be won/achieved); "Let the cat out of the bag" (to reveal a secret unintentionally).

• Similar idioms meaning "completely/entirely": lock, stock and barrel; from top to bottom.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

It is very difficult for her to ____________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. keep a secret.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "keep" collocates naturally with the noun "secret" in English — "to keep a secret" is the standard, idiomatic collocation meaning to not reveal information to others.

• Rule — Collocation: Certain verbs habitually pair with certain nouns in English (e.g. "keep a secret", "make a decision", "take a break"); using the wrong verb with a noun, even if individually correct words, produces an unnatural or meaningless expression.

• Applying the rule: "It is very difficult for her to keep a secret" is the only grammatically and idiomatically correct completion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "touch a secret" is incorrect because "touch" does not collocate with "secret"; "touch" is used with physical objects, not with abstract information like a secret.

• Option 3: "make a secret" is incorrect because the correct collocation for creating secrecy is "keep something secret" or "keep a secret", not "make a secret".

• Option 4: "cry a secret" is incorrect because "cry" is an intransitive verb of emotion/sound and cannot take "a secret" as its object in standard usage.

NOTE

• Common verb-noun collocations tested in SSC exams: keep a promise, keep a secret, make a decision, take a decision, pay attention, take care, do homework, make an effort.

• Always check which verb naturally pairs with the given noun rather than translating literally from another language.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Traffickng.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word is misspelled in option 3; the correct spelling is "Trafficking" — meaning the illegal trade or transportation of goods, drugs, or people.
◦ Example: The police cracked down on the human trafficking ring operating near the border.

• Spelling key: TRAFFIC + K + ING. When adding "-ing" to a short word ending in "-ic" ("traffic"), a "k" is inserted before "-ing" to preserve the hard "k" sound (traffic → trafficking, panic → panicking, picnic → picnicking). Option 3 wrongly drops the "i" before "-ng", giving "Traffickng" instead of "Trafficking".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Slaughter" is correctly spelled — meaning the killing of animals for food, or a brutal killing.

• Option 2: "Cropping" is correctly spelled — the present participle of "crop" (to cut short, or to grow a crop), formed by doubling the final consonant "p" before adding "-ing".

• Option 4: "Tyrannical" is correctly spelled — meaning cruel and oppressive, like a tyrant; note the double "n" and the ending "-ical".

NOTE

• Words ending in "-ic" take a "k" before "-ing", "-ed", or "-er": traffic → trafficking/trafficked; picnic → picnicking/picnicked; panic → panicking/panicked; mimic → mimicking/mimicked.

• Always check whether the final consonant before "-ing" needs doubling (as in "cropping") or an inserted "k" (as in "trafficking") based on the base word's ending.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom that can be substituted in the following sentence.

He was murdered in cold blood.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. deliberately.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "in cold blood" means done deliberately, without any feeling of pity or mercy, and often with careful planning. (ठंडे दिमाग से/जान-बूझकर, बिना किसी दया के)
◦ Example: The soldiers were shot in cold blood by the enemy forces.

• The idiom is most commonly used to describe murders or violent acts committed calmly and deliberately, without any emotion or hesitation, rather than in the heat of sudden anger.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in cold weather" is incorrect because it takes the phrase literally, referring to temperature, which is not the idiomatic meaning.

• Option 3: "when blood was cold" is incorrect for the same reason — it is a literal, nonsensical reading of the idiom rather than its figurative sense.

• Option 4: "regretfully" is incorrect because the idiom conveys deliberateness and lack of emotion/mercy, not a sense of regret or remorse.

NOTE

• Other common idioms using "blood": "Blood is thicker than water" (family bonds are stronger than other relationships); "Make one's blood boil" (to make someone very angry); "New blood" (new members bringing fresh energy to a group).

• Contrast with "in the heat of the moment", which means acting impulsively under strong emotion — the opposite of acting "in cold blood".

question:
Rectify the sentence by selecting the correct spelling of the underlined word.

David was put off by the glamming eyes in the dark.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. gleaming.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Gleaming" — meaning shining brightly, especially with reflected light; radiant.
◦ Example: The cat's gleaming eyes were visible even in the pitch-dark room.

• Spelling key: GLEAM + ING. The base word is "gleam" (to shine brightly), and "-ing" is added directly without doubling any letter. The misspelled word in the sentence, "glamming", incorrectly replaces "glea" with "glam", which is unrelated to the intended meaning.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "glamning" is incorrect; it is not a recognised English word and appears to be a random alteration of "gleaming".

• Option 2: "gleaning" is incorrect; although it looks similar, "gleaning" (from "glean") means collecting information or grain bit by bit, which does not fit the meaning of shining/bright eyes.

• Option 4: "glaming" is incorrect; it is not a standard English word and omits the required "e" of "gleam".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "gleam" (to shine) with "glean" (to gather information/grain gradually) — the two are frequently confused in spelling-based questions due to their similar letters.

• Other "-eam" words often tested: beam, cream, dream, steam, scream — all retain the "ea" digraph.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The planets are ________________ around the sun.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. revolving.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "revolve" specifically means to move in a circular or curving path around a central point/another object, which is the precise astronomical term for what planets do around the sun.

• Rule — Word choice/usage: In standard English (and specifically in scientific/astronomical usage), a planet's motion around the sun is called "revolving", while its spin on its own axis is called "rotating". Since the sentence uses "around the sun", the fitting verb is "revolving".

• Applying the rule: "The planets are revolving around the sun" is the standard, idiomatic, and scientifically accurate expression.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "circling" is a plausible-sounding but less precise/standard choice in this fixed astronomical context; "revolving around" is the conventionally accepted collocation for planetary motion, making it the better fit over the more generic "circling".

• Option 3: "rotating" is incorrect because "rotating" refers to a body spinning on its own axis (e.g. "The Earth rotates on its axis"), not to its orbital motion around another body.

• Option 4: "rounding" is incorrect because "rounding" means going around a corner/bend or approximating a number; it is not used to describe orbital motion.

NOTE

• Remember the key distinction: Rotate = spin on one's own axis (e.g., Earth rotates once every 24 hours); Revolve = move in orbit around another body (e.g., Earth revolves around the Sun once a year).

• This rotate/revolve distinction is a frequently tested vocabulary-usage point in SSC exams.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.

The child was / gazing longingly / at the toy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The child was gazing longingly at the toy" is in the Past Continuous Tense, correctly formed as Subject + was/were + V-ing.

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense: used to describe an action that was in progress at a particular time in the past; formed with "was/were" + the present participle (V-ing) of the main verb.

• Checking each part: "The child was" (correct subject + auxiliary for singular subject), "gazing longingly" (correct V-ing form + adverb of manner modifying the verb), "at the toy" (correct preposition "at" used with "gaze", as in "gaze at something"). All three parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error in the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "gazing longingly" is grammatically correct — "gazing" is the correct present participle, and "longingly" is the correctly formed adverb (adjective "longing" + "-ly") modifying it.

• Option 2: "at the toy" is grammatically correct — "gaze" correctly takes the preposition "at" (one gazes AT something), and "the toy" is a properly formed noun phrase.

• Option 4: "The child was" is grammatically correct — "was" is the correct singular past-tense auxiliary agreeing with the singular subject "the child".

NOTE

• Verbs of looking and their fixed prepositions: gaze AT, stare AT, look AT, glance AT/OVER, peer AT/INTO — using the wrong preposition with these verbs is a common SSC error-spotting trap.

• When no grammatical fault is found in any segment, always consider "No error" as a genuine possible answer rather than forcing an error where none exists.

question:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate word. Choose the correct alternative.
If you are the one who is planning to lose weight, remember to keep your snacking ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. moderate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "moderate" means kept within reasonable limits; not excessive. In the context of losing weight, the sentence logically advises keeping one's snacking limited/controlled, which is exactly what "moderate" conveys.

• Rule — Contextual word choice: the blank must be filled with a word that fits both the grammatical slot (an adjective describing "snacking") and the logical meaning of the sentence (advice for someone trying to lose weight).

• Applying the rule: "remember to keep your snacking moderate" makes complete logical sense — moderate snacking supports weight loss.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "outgoing" is incorrect because it means sociable/friendly in personality; it makes no sense describing "snacking".

• Option 2: "prejudiced" is incorrect because it means having a preconceived, biased opinion; it is unrelated to eating habits.

• Option 3: "uncontrolled" is incorrect because it means the opposite of what is logically advised — uncontrolled snacking would work against, not support, weight loss.

NOTE

• Contextual fill-in-the-blank questions require checking logical consistency with the whole sentence, not just grammatical correctness — here, three of the four options (outgoing, prejudiced, uncontrolled) are grammatically valid adjectives but only "moderate" fits the meaning.

• Similar exam-favoured words for "kept within limits": measured, restrained, controlled, temperate.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.

If writers only dared to dare, a Suetonius or a Tacitus of the Novel could exist, for the Novel is (1)_______________ the history of manners, turned into a story and a play, as is History itself often enough. And there is no other (2)_______________ than this: that the one, the Novel, cloaks its manners (3)_______________ the disguise of invented characters, while the other, History, (4)_______________ names and addresses. Only, the Novel (5)_______________ much deeper than History.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. essentially.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "essentially" means basically; in essence; at its core. In blank (1), the sentence states that the Novel is, at its very core/essence, the history of manners turned into a story — this is the central claim of the passage, which "essentially" captures precisely.

• Rule — Contextual vocabulary in cloze passages: each blank must be filled by considering the overall argument of the passage; here, the author is making a definitional claim about what the Novel fundamentally IS, which calls for a word meaning "fundamentally/basically", not one implying choice or lack of necessity.

• Applying the rule: "the Novel is essentially the history of manners..." fits the passage's definitional, assertive tone.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "optionally" is incorrect because it implies the Novel being the history of manners is a matter of choice, which contradicts the passage's assertive, definitional tone.

• Option 2: "needlessly" is incorrect because it means "without necessity/unnecessarily", which makes no logical sense when defining what the Novel fundamentally is.

• Option 4: "unnecessarily" is incorrect for the same reason as "needlessly" — it suggests something uncalled for, which does not fit a statement defining the essential nature of the Novel.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the full passage first to grasp the author's tone (here, assertive/definitional) before choosing a word for each blank.

• Words similar to "essentially": fundamentally, basically, inherently, intrinsically.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.

If writers only dared to dare, a Suetonius or a Tacitus of the Novel could exist, for the Novel is (1)_______________ the history of manners, turned into a story and a play, as is History itself often enough. And there is no other (2)_______________ than this: that the one, the Novel, cloaks its manners (3)_______________ the disguise of invented characters, while the other, History, (4)_______________ names and addresses. Only, the Novel (5)_______________ much deeper than History.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. difference.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is followed by "than this", forming the phrase **"no other ______ than this", which requires a noun that can be compared using "than" — "difference"** fits naturally, as the sentence goes on to explain exactly what distinguishes the Novel and History.

• Rule — Contextual vocabulary in cloze passages: the word chosen must grammatically combine with "than this" and must also match the explanation that follows (the sentence explains HOW the Novel and History differ), confirming that "difference" is the required noun.

• Applying the rule: "there is no other difference than this: that the one, the Novel, cloaks its manners...while the other, History,..." — the sentence explicitly lists a point of contrast, i.e. a difference.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "pragmatism" is incorrect because it means a practical, results-focused approach; it does not fit the comparative structure "no other ______ than this".

• Option 3: "matter" is incorrect because although grammatically it could fit loosely, it does not capture the explicitly contrastive/comparative sense that the following clause (introduced by "that... while...") demands.

• Option 4: "sample" is incorrect because it means a small representative part of something, which is unrelated to the comparison being drawn between the Novel and History.

NOTE

• Phrases like "no other ______ than this" are strong contextual clues — look at what follows the colon to identify exactly what kind of noun is required.

• "Difference" is followed by "between X and Y" or explained by a "that...while..." clause, as seen here.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.

If writers only dared to dare, a Suetonius or a Tacitus of the Novel could exist, for the Novel is (1)_______________ the history of manners, turned into a story and a play, as is History itself often enough. And there is no other (2)_______________ than this: that the one, the Novel, cloaks its manners (3)_______________ the disguise of invented characters, while the other, History, (4)_______________ names and addresses. Only, the Novel (5)_______________ much deeper than History.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. under.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase **"cloaks its manners _____ the disguise of" requires a preposition that means covered by/hidden beneath — "under"** is the standard preposition used with "disguise" and "cloak" (to cloak something under a disguise = to hide it beneath a disguise).

• Rule — Fixed prepositional usage: certain verbs/nouns take fixed prepositions; "cloak...under" and "under the disguise of" are conventional English collocations meaning to conceal something by means of a disguise.

• Applying the rule: "the Novel cloaks its manners under the disguise of invented characters" is the grammatically standard and idiomatic expression.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "beside" is incorrect because it means "next to", which does not fit the sense of concealment implied by "cloaks" and "disguise".

• Option 3: "around" is incorrect because "cloaks...around" would suggest wrapping something on the outside, not hiding it beneath a disguise, and does not collocate with "disguise".

• Option 4: "among" is incorrect because it means "in the middle of a group", which is grammatically and logically unsuitable here since "disguise" is singular, not a group.

NOTE

• Common fixed prepositional phrases: "under the guise of", "under the disguise of", "under the pretext of" — all mean concealed by means of something.

• Always check whether the noun following the blank (here "disguise") demands a specific fixed preposition.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.

If writers only dared to dare, a Suetonius or a Tacitus of the Novel could exist, for the Novel is (1)_______________ the history of manners, turned into a story and a play, as is History itself often enough. And there is no other (2)_______________ than this: that the one, the Novel, cloaks its manners (3)_______________ the disguise of invented characters, while the other, History, (4)_______________ names and addresses. Only, the Novel (5)_______________ much deeper than History.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. provides.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence contrasts the Novel (which invents/disguises characters) with History, which, unlike the Novel, deals in real, factual identities — that is, History "provides" (gives/supplies) real names and addresses.

• Rule — Contextual logic in cloze passages: the word must fit the contrast set up by "while" — the Novel HIDES identity behind invented characters, whereas History does the opposite and openly GIVES real names and addresses; "provides" captures this positive, supplying sense.

• Applying the rule: "while the other, History, provides names and addresses" completes the intended contrast logically and grammatically.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "negates" is incorrect because it means "cancels out/nullifies", which does not fit — History does not negate names and addresses, it supplies them.

• Option 3: "removes" is incorrect because it means "takes away", which is the opposite of what History does with real names and addresses in this contrast.

• Option 4: "strangulates" is incorrect because it literally means "to choke/strangle", which is nonsensical when applied to "names and addresses".

NOTE

• In contrast structures using "while"/"whereas", identify what the first clause says and look for a word that expresses the logical opposite or complementary action in the second clause.

• "Provide" collocates naturally with information-type nouns: provide details, provide names, provide evidence, provide addresses.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.

If writers only dared to dare, a Suetonius or a Tacitus of the Novel could exist, for the Novel is (1)_______________ the history of manners, turned into a story and a play, as is History itself often enough. And there is no other (2)_______________ than this: that the one, the Novel, cloaks its manners (3)_______________ the disguise of invented characters, while the other, History, (4)_______________ names and addresses. Only, the Novel (5)_______________ much deeper than History.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. probes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "probes" means examines or investigates something thoroughly and deeply. The sentence states that the Novel goes "much deeper than History", and "probes" is the verb that best expresses this idea of deep investigation/exploration.

• Rule — Contextual vocabulary in cloze passages: the word chosen must logically connect with the phrase that follows it, "much deeper than History" — only a verb of deep examination/investigation like "probes" naturally combines with "deeper".

• Applying the rule: "Only, the Novel probes much deeper than History" conveys that the Novel investigates human character and manners more deeply than factual History does.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "bargains" is incorrect because it means "negotiates a price/deal", which is unrelated to the idea of exploring something "deeper".

• Option 2: "listens" is incorrect because "listens...deeper" is not idiomatic; listening relates to sound/attention, not depth of investigation into manners.

• Option 4: "imbibes" is incorrect because it means "absorbs/takes in (ideas or liquid)", which does not logically combine with "much deeper than History" in the sense of investigation.

NOTE

• "Probe" is commonly used with "deep/deeper/into": to probe deeply into a matter, to probe a mystery, a probing question.

• In cloze passages, always check which verb most naturally collocates with the words immediately surrounding the blank (here, "much deeper than").
